newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Devolution stirs passion, finally, in Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Devolution stirs passion, finally, in Britain.

text.p: Mention devolution to people in England and their eyes usually glaze over. But if the topic arises in Scotland or Wales an impassioned debate is guaranteed.

Since Wales was united with England in 1536 and Scotland followed in 1707, the two nations have clamoured for greater autonomy from London. Historical, cultural, legal and linguistic differences are cited as the main reasons.

Apart from the occasional failed uprising, moves for independence and more self-rule have simmered beneath the surface, and been defeated when tested at the polls. But with an election due by May 22 and the ruling Conservatives likely to be ousted after 18 years in government, nationalists have once again raised their heads and voices.

Prime Minister John Major has made devolution a key election issue saying there is "clear blue water" between his Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party because of his fierce defence of the "Union" of the countries that make up Britain.
Labour has promised to give Wales and Scotland their own mini-parliaments, partly through conviction and partly to attract votes from the nationalist parties.

Suddenly devolution is being discussed throughout Britain and nowhere more eloquently than at the Oxford Union, the renowned debating club of one of Britain's greatest universities and a training ground for future politicians.
OXFORD UNION DEBATE

In the wood-panelled, galleried chamber, six politicians and students from all sides of the political spectrum this month debated the pros and cons of devolution to the cheers and jeers of the 400-member audience.
"Scotland and Wales should be given their own parliaments elected by proportional representation," said Jeremy Breaks, the kilted student who began the debate.
"Scotland and Wales are nations within a state. There are different educational and legal systems in Scotland and a different language in Wales."
Far from leading to the breakup of Britain, Breaks argued that devolution would strengthen ties with England by giving people the limited change that they want.
"It's about strengthening the union of states," agreed George Robertson, Labour spokesman for Scotland. "It is about recognising and responding to the will of the people."

Cynog Dafis, a member of parliament and member of the Plaid Cymru Welsh nationalist party, argued that Wales is a distinct country and criticised Labour's plans for an assembly in Cardiff with no legislative powers.
"We need the powers and we need them now. It will give us responsibility for our patch of the world," he said.

While Labour has long championed a parliament in Scotland and an assembly in Wales and has promised referendums if they win the election, the Conservatives have dismissed any idea of constitutional change as a dangerous proposition and the first step on the slippery slope to separatism.

The latest opinion poll showed 80 percent of Scots, who have 72 seats in the House of Commons in London, support a change in the constitution. Feelings in Wales, which sent 38 representatives to parliament, were running along similar lines.

Alex Salmond, leader of the pro-independent Scottish National Party, spoke of the anti-Scottish sentiment of the Conservative Party. With 30 percent of the vote in Scotland, the SNP trails Labour's 48 percent but is miles ahead of the Conservatives who have just 15 percent support.
"The Tory party wants to hang on to Scotland and Scottish resources," said Salmond, who has claimed that an independent Scotland would be the 21st richest country in the world.
"Independence would be the best thing for Scotland."
In response to the government's claims that it has brought more jobs to the nation, he replied. "There are plenty of jobs but all are at slave wages."
After listening to the arguments in support of more self-rule, William Hague, the balding yet boyish Secretary of State for Wales, warned of "delusion on a grand scale."
"It's a fundamental political error to think that you can meet half way those that want to tear it (the union) apart."
Robinson responded by accusing the Conservatives of denying the Scottish and Welsh people the devolution that they want. "Scottish people don't want separatism, they want devoltuion."
GOVERNMENT CASE
It was left to the Michael Forsyth, Secretary of State for Scotland, to drill home the government's case.

"It's the gerrymandering (manipulation) of our constitution that is at stake," he bellowed, adding that devolution was the most fundamental threat to the constitution since the English Civil War in the 16th century.
"The maintenance of the United Kingdom is the main priority...we must save our heritage," he warned.
In accordance with the century old tradition, the assembled audience cast their vote for the devolution proposition by leaving through the appropriate doors -- ayes to the right and noes to the left.
Long after their illustrious guests had left the votes were finally counted. At 228 to 189 the noes, those opposed to giving Scotland and Wales their own parliaments, won.
Voters in Scotland and Wales will still have their say, sometime between now and the end of May when Major must put his party's policies to the test.
